title: Monte Verde archaeological site
summary: Monte Verde, beside Chinchihuapi Creek in southern Chile, was long dated to about 14,500 years ago and treated as a leading pre-Clovis site in the Americas. A 2026 study in Science argues its archaeological layer is no older than the Middle Holocene; the new date is disputed.

uncertainty.note: The original dating is about 14,500 BP (year -12550 with year = 1950 minus BP). The 2026 study says the site cannot be older than 8200-4200 BP (about -6250 to -2250). Dating contested since March 2026; the range spans both.

as_recorded.calendar: Years before present (B.P.), original dates as reported in 2026

as_recorded.value: cannot be older than the Middle Holocene (8200 to 4200 years B.P.)

when.display: Dated c. 14,500 BP originally; reassessed in 2026 as no older than 8200-4200 BP (contested)

where.modern_name: Monte Verde, near Puerto Montt, Los Lagos Region, Chile
where.historical_name: No polity; hunter-gatherer camp on a creek in temperate rainforest of southern Chile

importance.justification: Its original date reshaped views of the first peopling of the Americas; the contested re-dating makes it central to current debate.

sources.title: A mid-Holocene age for Monte Verde challenges the timeline of human colonization of South America (Science, DOI 10.1126/science.adw9217)
sources.author: Todd A. Surovell, Cesar Mendez, Juan Luis Garcia, Christopher Luthgens, Jay M. Thompson, Claudio Latorre

sources.title: When did humans arrive in the Americas? A new study reignites the debate
